title: Teachers’ perceptions and uses of generative artificial intelligence in Moroccan schools: Evidence from the Fez–Meknès region
extended_summary:
This paper examines teachers’ awareness, perceptions, and actual use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in schools, addressing a gap in empirical evidence from Morocco. The authors focus on how in-service teachers understand generative AI, what they think it can do for teaching and learning, what barriers limit use, and what kinds of professional development they want.

The study uses a descriptive cross-sectional survey of 420 primary and secondary school teachers in Morocco’s Fez–Meknès region. Participants came from multiple subject areas and completed an online questionnaire covering general understanding of generative AI, current use, perceived contributions, useful applications, challenges, and training preferences. Data were analyzed descriptively using frequencies and percentages.

Findings show that most teachers had heard of generative AI and generally viewed it positively, especially for content creation, personalization, engagement, and support for lesson design. However, regular classroom use was much lower than perceived usefulness, largely because of limited training, weak infrastructure, and privacy concerns. Teachers also preferred hands-on workshops, live classroom applications, and coaching, and many saw generative AI as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for teachers. The paper concludes that targeted professional development, better infrastructure, and clear ethical guidelines are needed to translate interest into effective and responsible use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model tools that can create text and other content, support personalized learning, and assist with feedback or assessment tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed primary and secondary teachers’ awareness, perceived usefulness, actual use, perceived contributions, challenges, and training preferences regarding generative AI in teaching and lesson design.

findings.finding_summary: Among 420 primary and secondary teachers in Morocco’s Fez–Meknès region, 68.9% reported having heard of generative AI and 64.4% accurately defined it as a content-generation technology. Teachers’ perceptions were generally favorable, with 72.5% saying it is useful for improving education and 81.1% viewing it as an essential part of the educational process.
findings.measure: Teacher awareness, definition accuracy, perceived usefulness, future outlook

findings.finding_summary: Only 21.5% reported frequent use, while 18.8% used generative AI occasionally and 37.6% had not yet tried it. The most valued applications were creating educational materials (36.4%), customizing teaching methods (20.5%), and creating personalized assessments (17.9%).
findings.measure: Frequency of actual use; preferred/useful applications for teaching

findings.finding_summary: Teachers most often reported that generative AI could customize educational content (23.4%), provide innovative and dynamic content (22.5%), enhance student engagement (21.4%), and support interactive motivation tools (21.1%).

The leading barriers were lack of training and knowledge (27.3%) and lack of technical resources and infrastructure (25.7%), followed by privacy and data security concerns (15.2%). Despite this, 82.6% expressed interest in additional training, and 34.2% preferred workshops/training sessions while 29.2% preferred hands-on/live classroom applications.
findings.measure: Challenges, training interest, preferred professional development methods

findings.finding_summary: Regarding role concerns, 45.6% did not fear generative AI would reduce their role, 24.8% expressed concern, and 29.5% were unsure. For equity, 52.0% believed generative AI could foster educational equity, while 40.5% were unsure and 7.4% disagreed.
findings.measure: Fear of role reduction; perception of educational equity

quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive cross-sectional survey with self-reported perceptions and usage data, not an experimental or quasi-experimental impact study. Evidence is informative for needs assessment but is correlational and context-specific.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong perceived value and training demand, but no causal effect sizes or learning outcomes are measured. Observed impacts are therefore unclear rather than demonstrated.
